uncited: This article defines the hardware constraints and architectural trends that dictate the efficiency of volume rendering and ray tracing implementations.
It addresses the problem of mapping computational tasks to modern parallel hardware (CPUs and GPUs) by highlighting the trade-offs between compute intensity and memory latency.

What sets this family apart is its focus on the physical limitations of execution units—such as restricted branching in GPU fragment programs and the unsuitability of complex traversal algorithms for GPUs—rather than just algorithmic complexity.
This family does not define specific algorithmic variants but rather establishes the hardware context for its children.
Moreover, the current trend is to implement rendering methods on GPUs.
Purcell et al. [PBMH02] showed that it is possible to do ray tracing with programmable graphics hardware.
Further works have been made by using different data structures such as kd-tree or BVH.
The traversal algorithm is unsuited for GPU computation, and branching is unavoidable.
